Faceless Studio · Gemini composition

The brief is the work

You were right. Given a brief that names every element, its position, its ink and what sits in front of what, Gemini composes a better thumbnail than my HTML compositor does — and not marginally.

Mine, then Gemini’s, from the same brief

Shown at 320 pixels. Same story, same number, same palette, same instructions — one arranged by CSS, one drawn.

What made the difference — the brief, not the model

The same account produced a scale bar it invented out of nothing a few weeks ago. What changed is how much of the work was done before the request.

The print process, first and at length

Every earlier failure came from leaving it implied. Duotone, one dot pitch across every element, hard offset shadows with no blur, paper grain, slight ink misregistration — written as a process, not as a mood. It is the longest section of the brief and it governs everything after it.

Every element placed, not described

Which quadrant. What percentage of the frame width. How many degrees of rotation. Which edge crops it. What sits in front of what. “It sits in the LOWER LEFT and is deliberately CROPPED by both the left edge and the bottom edge, so roughly a fifth of the coin runs off the picture.”

An ink budget, as a hard limit

Three hex values, named, with “no fourth colour anywhere”. Restriction is what made the reference hold together, so it is stated as a rule rather than left to taste.

Type given verbatim, line by line

Each line with its position down the frame, its colour, and its size as a fraction of frame height — then “spell all three lines exactly as written. Do not add any other words, numbers or symbols.” That is what got the typography back correct.

A forbidden list taken from real failures

Smooth gradients, soft blurred shadows, a fourth ink, anything floating with space around it, centred type — and any invented number, date, statistic, unit or currency symbol not written out in the brief.

The source photograph attached, with its lighting released

“Match the object’s shape, proportions and markings exactly, because this is a real thing… do NOT copy its lighting, background or framing.” That is the line that keeps a real coin from becoming a model’s idea of one.

3.69 cents to make one cent

Two coins, both cropped by frame edges, halftone following the relief of the portrait. Gemini’s type block is larger and locked tighter; the contrast on the copper is far stronger than my duotone ramp achieved.

$7.25, frozen since 2009

The clearest win of the set. My dome is a flat blue silhouette; Gemini’s is an engraved screen print at nearly twice the size, running off two edges, with the stars sitting quietly under it rather than competing.

690,000 — they all ran

A pasted photographic print, screened to steel, with the stamp knocked off the grid.

And then both at once

Each thumbnail was ordered twice — once complete, once with the clear half left deliberately empty. Gemini draws the plate; our own Anton headline drops into the space afterwards. That buys back the one thing the prompt could not have: an exact glyph. Note the real ¢ sign, which I would not risk asking a model to set.

gemini plate + our type
gemini plate + our type

Where Gemini wins

Ink that sits on the field

The dome is a genuine engraved screen-print: halftone following the curve of the drum, columns as hard strokes, cream highlights biting out of the blue. CSS can posterise a photograph. It cannot draw that.

Type with printed edges

Gemini’s letterforms are tighter, the offset shadow more confident, and the two lines lock as one mark. Mine are a speckle mask over a webfont, which is a reasonable imitation of the same idea.

Scale it is not afraid of

Given “about 65 percent of the frame width, cropped by two edges”, it commits. My layout kept flinching and pulling the subject back inside the frame.

Where the compositor still wins

Exactness

I asked for 3.69 CENTS rather than 3.69¢ because a cent sign was a risk not worth taking. The compositor sets whatever glyph I want, every time.

Reproducibility

The same spec renders the same frame forever. A prompt returns a different picture each run, and a border it was told twice not to draw.

Cost and speed

Instant and free against a subscription credit and a two-to-three minute wait per image. For the section cards and in-video graphics, that settles it.

So both stay, with a clean split. Thumbnails go to Gemini — there is one per video, quality is the entire point, and a subscription credit is the right thing to spend it on. Section cards, stat cards and in-video graphics stay with the compositor, where hundreds of frames need to be exact, free, instant and identical on every re-render. The Gemini path now also orders a text-free twin of each thumbnail, so our own Anton headline can be dropped into the empty half whenever the burnt-in type comes back wrong.
Two practical notes. Output arrives at 2752×1536 — off 16:9 — and often carries a pale border despite the brief forbidding one in as many words; fvs/trim.py removes both, and only treats a band as a border when it appears on all four sides, or artwork that runs to the edge gets eaten from the outside in. And 690,000 still needs its source check before it ships: NHTSA’s final count is nearer 677,000.
